claims.statement: The release-please package registry is the source for the nine managed components and their changelog targets; the manifest baselines are Deep Agents 0.7.41, ACP 0.1.0, Code 0.2.14, Talon 0.1.2, Daytona 0.0.9, Modal 0.0.8, Runloop 0.0.7, Vercel 0.0.2, and QuickJS 0.4.0.

The lockfile refresh helper recalculates `uv.lock` for each changed manifest owner and its transitive local-source consumers, using the package-specific Python resolver policy; the checker only tests directly touched packages unless invoked with no paths, when it tests all discovered packages.

Code publishes an exact `deepagents==0.7.41` dependency but substitutes the editable `../deepagents` checkout in its workspace configuration, so local development does not validate the SDK distribution version PyPI users receive.

Talon publishes Python 3.14-only compatibility and declares `deepagents>=0.7.41` plus `deepagents-code>=0.2.14,<1.0.0`; local source mappings remain development wiring rather than published dependency metadata.

Package manifests are published compatibility contracts while `[tool.uv.sources]` mappings are editable checkout-only wiring; contributors work inside the owning package and use package-local uv environments and Make targets.

The release-please workflow installs and runs a pinned, pnpm-patched local runner rather than the prebuilt action; installation fails if the patch no longer applies, and the runner verifies the file-exclusion and `==` tag-parsing patches before making GitHub calls.

The local release-please runner replaces the GraphQL history walk with a full-history blobless-clone `git log` iterator, removes the 500-commit cap, reconstructs PR data from squash or merge subjects, uses override PR bodies when present, and represents first-parent merge files and both rename paths for path-based release attribution.

Release processing rejects empty commits because they have no paths to scope, dispatches publishing for detected release commits before release-PR maintenance, and waits for repo-wide pending publishes to reach a known-safe state before the serialized runner recomputes release PRs.

A bump-worthy PR that changes release-relevant files in multiple configured components is blocked by the scope workflow unless explicitly acknowledged with `ci:allow-lockfile-release`; it reads trusted base configuration, excludes package tests and `uv.lock`, and fails closed when the GitHub changed-file list is incomplete.

When release-please creates or updates release PRs, its workflow regenerates every tracked `uv.lock` on each release branch and retries a rejected branch push by fetching, regenerating, and committing again up to three times.

The curated-notes workflow derives the release target from a trusted internal release branch and matching title, runs automation from `main`, and requires a ready release PR plus write-level maintainer permission for manual `@release-bot` commands.

Curated-note drafting treats release-branch text as untrusted, binds the draft to validated release state, hides the generated `### Dependencies` section from the model, and restores that section verbatim so dependency metadata cannot be edited through prose curation.

Applying curated notes fails rather than writing when trusted draft state is stale or altered, including changed generated entries, heading or dependency edits, untrusted bot metadata, branch changes, and concurrent PR updates.

The release-branch lockfile job generates the dependency changelog subsection by diffing `pyproject.toml` from the resolved predecessor tag to the release head; generation warns and leaves the changelog unchanged on errors, so it does not block lockfile updates.

The local release-body builder resolves a reachable predecessor tag, extracts the version-specific changelog section at the release SHA, and produces bounded, escaped package-scoped Git history so a release body does not attribute later commits or unsafe text.

The dispatch-only release workflow validates a normal release SHA is reachable from `main` and declares the requested version, builds that exact detached tree, verifies downloaded artifact checksums, then publishes through TestPyPI and PyPI before creating the package-version tag and GitHub release.

A release-notes failure is intentionally fail-open: publishing and tagging continue with an empty GitHub release body, while the tagging job reports a recovery command that rebuilds the body locally for the exact release SHA and applies it with `gh release edit --notes-file`.

Once a package version has reached PyPI, maintainers must not move or recreate its tag; a failed pre-publication release can be recovered by dispatching the workflow for a hotfix SHA that retains the target version, whereas a post-publication defect requires a new release version.
